newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya's president tries to defuse reform pressure.
newsitem.headline: Kenya's president tries to defuse reform pressure.

text.p: President Daniel arap Moi has met Kenya's religious leaders in a bid to defuse pressure for political reforms that ignited bloody clashes between police and protesters.
But he stopped well short of opposition-backed demands.

In his first meeting with religious leaders on reforms since an opposition-backed campaign took to the streets of Nairobi in June, the official Presidential Press Service (PPS) said Moi and clerics on Tuesday agreed on a need for constitutional review.
The PPS said they agreed it was necessary to review the constitution "with a view to amending or overhauling it to serve the needs, requirements and aspirations of modern Kenya".
But the PPS added: "The time and mechanism for effecting these changes will be discussed in subsequent meetings."
Opposition parties, human rights and other groups seek a list of what they say are "minimal" reforms before elections and have vowed to escalate their campaign until they are approved.
"This is one of the signs Moi is cracking," said a leading opposition activist, who declined to be identified. "We hope this is the start of progress towards the reforms we want."
"It's a move in the right direction but we will have to see what it amounts to," said a senior Kenyan political analyst.

The churches have been a major force behind the drive this year for the constitutional reforms, which would weaken the power of Moi, 73 and Kenya's ruler for 19 years. No date has yet been set for this year's presidential and parliamentary polls.
The PPS said Moi and the clerics, including Kenya's Catholic and Anglican archbishops and its chief Moslem Kadhi, agreed violence should be condemned and confrontation eliminated.
It said Moi's government would review the legislative and administrative framework to ensure free and fair elections and the religious leaders would make proposals to the government.
But more unrest was reported by students late on Tuesday at Egerton University, an agricultural college 180 km (110 miles) northwest of Nairobi. Few details were available.

Earlier, polytechnic students calling for political reforms and Moi's departure from office clashed sporadically with police in the heart of Kenya's capital for a second day, but violence was much lighter than on Monday.
Kenyan opposition politician Richard Leakey told Reuters the Indian Ocean port city of Mombasa was the next target for the reform campaign.
Leakey, secretary-general of the unregistered Safina party, said the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC) behind the reformers sought agreement from the government this month.
"The NCEC is coordinating...and Mombasa has been identified as the next major event," said Leakey, an NCEC member, Kenya's former wildlife guardian and a renowned palaeontologist.

"We are conscious that Mombasa could turn very violent and are very conscious of the consequences," said Leakey. Mombasa is at the centre of Kenya's tourism industry, the country's main foreign exchange earner.
At least nine people were killed in Kenya on July 7 during the country's worst political violence in seven years when riot police broke up a day of demonstrations called by the NCEC.
The July 7 violence, which closed down Nairobi, was followed by student unrest in the capital last week, leading to closure of two universities followed by Kenya Polytechnic on Monday.
In Mombasa, fiery Moslem preacher Sheikh Khalid Balala who says he will boycott the elections vowed on Tuesday to burn voter registration cards from next Friday to press for reforms.
Balala, perhaps the most outspoken opponent of the Kenyan president, told reporters in his home city he would pay 10 Kenyan shillings for every registration card to be burned.
But Balala, allowed to return to Kenya by authorities on Saturday after two years of exile in Germany, has proved more extreme than the NCEC, which is loathe to boycott the polls.
He even on Tuesday met some resistance from his mother.
"I shall stitch his mouth up unless he tones it down," Fatima Sadik bin Salem told reporters in front of her son. ($1=58.78 Kenyan shillings)
